# 1. Reliability: can you trust the judge? {#reliability-can-you-trust-the-instrument .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<p class="j2-sec-goal"><span>Learning goal 1</span>Before we trust a judge, we test it. We ask four things.</p>
<p class="j2-colhead j2-sec-head">In this section</p>
<ol class="j2-sec-list">
  <li><a href="#/the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict"><span>1.1</span>Does it give the same answer twice?</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter"><span>1.2</span>Does it ignore things that don't matter?</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer"><span>1.3</span>Does it agree with people?</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof"><span>1.4</span>Are its reasons good?</a></li>
</ol>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** A judge is a measurement instrument. Before its numbers mean anything, it has to give the same answer to the same case, ignore what should not matter, agree with people on this task, and give reasons that hold up. This section takes those four in turn.
:::

---

## Does it give the same answer twice? {#the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 1, Reliability: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/reliability-can-you-trust-the-instrument"><span>1</span>Reliability</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict"><span>1.1</span>Consistency</a><a href="#/verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter"><span>1.2</span>Robustness</a><a href="#/agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer"><span>1.3</span>Transfer</a><a href="#/a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof"><span>1.4</span>Explanations</a></nav>
<div class="j2-split j2-split-even">
  <div class="j2-panel">
    <p class="j2-colhead">Same answers, different order</p>
    <p class="j2-metric">How often the judge changed its mind when the two answers were swapped</p>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Close cases</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-bad" style="width:71.4%"></span></span><b>25 of 35</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Clear cases</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:2.6%"></span></span><b>1 of 39</b></div>
    <p class="j2-src"><a href="../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/">Wang et al. 2024</a></p>
  </div>
  <div class="j2-panel fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
    <p class="j2-colhead">Can we fix it by running the judge many times? A little.</p>
    <p class="j2-metric">Ties, with 1 run and with 16 runs</p>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">1 run</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-ref" style="width:26.7%"></span></span><b>26.7%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">16 runs</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:5.5%"></span></span><b>5.5%</b></div>
    <p class="j2-src"><a href="../../bibliography/kwok-2026-llm-as-verifier/">Kwok et al. 2026</a>. Accuracy goes up by less than three points (74.7% to 77.5%).</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="j2-note fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>Don't report one run. Report the spread.</b> The spread shows you where the judge is unsure, and that's where you should look.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Inconsistency is not spread evenly. A judge is stable on clear cases and unstable on close ones, which are the cases where a verdict matters. Repeating a judgement reduces ties but costs calls and buys little accuracy.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on close and clear cases, then (1) repeats, and (2) report the spread.
- Wang et al.: with the two answers swapped, 25 of 35 close comparisons flipped, against 1 of 39 clear ones ([Wang et al. 2024](../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/)). Close means the two answers were near in quality.
- Kwok et al.: a judge that prints one integer tied on 26.7% of comparisons at one pass and 5.5% at 16 passes; pairwise accuracy rose from 74.7% to 77.5% ([Kwok et al. 2026](../../bibliography/kwok-2026-llm-as-verifier/)). Part 2's slide 2.4 used the accuracy figure for cost; here the point is what repeats reveal.
- The same holds for agent judges: the same judge on the same trace can differ across runs ([Voss 2026](../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/)).
- Temperature 0 makes output repeatable, not right (Part 2, tip in 3.4). The Part 3 app defaults to temperature 0 and one repeat, and allows up to five repeats; each repeat is an independent trace evaluation (workshop/README.md).
:::

## Does it ignore things that don't matter? {#verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 1, Reliability: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/reliability-can-you-trust-the-instrument"><span>1</span>Reliability</a><a href="#/the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict"><span>1.1</span>Consistency</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter"><span>1.2</span>Robustness</a><a href="#/agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer"><span>1.3</span>Transfer</a><a href="#/a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof"><span>1.4</span>Explanations</a></nav>
<table class="j2-tbl j2-tbl-fail">
  <thead><tr><th>Change one small thing</th><th>What happened</th><th>Source</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Give the judge more answers to compare</td><td>With 3 or 4 answers instead of 2, most judges got confused by the order (position robustness below 0.5)</td><td><a href="../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/">Ye et al. 2024</a></td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><td>Write the wrong answer in fluent English</td><td>GPT-4 picked the right answer 88% of the time on normal pairs, but only 37% when the wrong answer was fluent</td><td><a href="../../bibliography/zhou-2024-mitigating-bias/">Zhou et al. 2024</a></td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><td>Give an empty answer, just “Yes”</td><td>Some small judges said: correct!</td><td><a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a></td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><td>The judge is not sure</td><td>Almost every judge said “correct”</td><td><a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<div class="j2-note fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><b>Researchers tested twelve biases. No judge passed all twelve,</b> and the best judge overall was not the best on every test (<a href="../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/">Ye et al. 2024</a>). Don't choose a judge by its famous name. Choose it by how it behaves on your task.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Robustness means the verdict stays put when something irrelevant changes. Each row changes one thing and shows the verdict moving. The method is the lesson: probe a judge one factor at a time.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: one probe per click: opens on adding answers, then (1) a fluent miss, (2) empty answers, (3) leniency, and (4) no judge is robust to everything.
- Ye et al. (CALM): 12 biases, injected one at a time, on six judges (ChatGPT, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5, GLM-4, Qwen2-72B). Claude-3.5 was the most resilient overall, yet not on every bias. Position robustness fell below 0.5 for most models with three or four answers, which warns against widening a pairwise judge into a ranking judge ([Ye et al. 2024](../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/)).
- Zhou et al. (LLMBar): GPT-4 scored 88.00 on the Natural set and 37.31 on Neighbor, where the tempting answer is close to the request but does not follow it. One accuracy on ordinary data hides the bias ([Zhou et al. 2024](../../bibliography/zhou-2024-mitigating-bias/)).
- Thakur et al.: on TriviaQA, judges such as Llama-2 13B and Gemma 2B often passed the dummy answers “Yes” and “Sure”, and some rejected a verbatim gold answer. Almost all judges showed leniency bias, P₊ > 0.5 ([Thakur et al. 2024](../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/)).
- Part 2's manipulation row (a four-word phrase lifting scores from 3.73 to 4.74, [Raina et al. 2024](../../bibliography/raina-2024-robust-judge/)) is the adversarial version of the same problem.
- These are text judges on single answers. None of these studies measures a judge reading agent traces, so treat them as lower bounds on what can go wrong there.
:::

## Does it agree with people? {#agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 1, Reliability: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/reliability-can-you-trust-the-instrument"><span>1</span>Reliability</a><a href="#/the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict"><span>1.1</span>Consistency</a><a href="#/verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter"><span>1.2</span>Robustness</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer"><span>1.3</span>Transfer</a><a href="#/a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof"><span>1.4</span>Explanations</a></nav>
<div class="j2-split j2-split-even">
  <div class="j2-panel">
    <p class="j2-colhead">An easy task, simple trivia questions. Judges are still below people.</p>
    <p class="j2-metric">Agreement with people (Scott's π), TriviaQA, correct or not</p>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">People with people</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-ref" style="width:96%"></span></span><b>96</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Llama-3 70B</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:88%"></span></span><b>88</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">GPT-4 Turbo</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:87%"></span></span><b>87</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">JudgeLM 7B</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:65%"></span></span><b>65</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">“Contains” rule</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:64%"></span></span><b>64</b></div>
    <p class="j2-src"><a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a></p>
  </div>
  <div class="j2-side">
    <p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>Agreement changes from task to task.</b> It depends on what you rate, who rates it, and who wrote the text (<a href="../../bibliography/bavaresco-2025-human-judges/">Bavaresco et al. 2025</a>).</p>
    <p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>Judges agree with experts mostly on questions they can answer themselves.</b> In finance, a reference answer mostly fixed this. Give your judge something to check against (<a href="../../bibliography/krumdick-2025-no-free-labels/">Krumdick et al. 2025</a>).</p>
    <p class="j2-strong fragment" data-fragment-index="3">A paper says “our judge agrees with people”. On which task? Test it on your task, with your people.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Agreement with people is a property of a judge on a task, not of a judge. It falls as the task gets less clear-cut or more expert, and it collapses where the judge does not know the answer itself.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on the TriviaQA figures, then (1) it varies by task, (2) it tracks what the judge knows, and (3) validate on your task.
- Thakur et al. chose TriviaQA because people agree on it (98.33% raw, Scott's π about 96), so any gap is the judge's. GPT-4 Turbo (87) and Llama-3 70B (88) led and still trailed people by about 8 points; JudgeLM 7B (65) barely beat the lexical “Contains” check (64) ([Thakur et al. 2024](../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/)). This is the easy case.
- Bavaresco et al. (JUDGE-BENCH): 20 NLP datasets with human labels, 11 open and proprietary judges; reliability varied with the property rated, the expertise of the human raters, and whether the text was human or model-written. Their conclusion: validate against human judgements before use ([Bavaresco et al. 2025](../../bibliography/bavaresco-2025-human-judges/)).
- Krumdick et al. (BFF-Bench, 160 finance questions, 1,200 expert-judged responses): without a correct reference, judges agreed highly with experts only on questions they could answer themselves; expert references largely mitigated it ([Krumdick et al. 2025](../../bibliography/krumdick-2025-no-free-labels/)). This is why Part 2 said “give it something to check against”.
- Part 2's expert result belongs here too: dietitians agreed with an LLM judge 68% of the time, psychologists 64% ([Szymanski et al. 2025](../../bibliography/szymanski-2025-expert-tasks/)).
:::

## Are its reasons good? {#a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 1, Reliability: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/reliability-can-you-trust-the-instrument"><span>1</span>Reliability</a><a href="#/the-same-case-can-get-a-different-verdict"><span>1.1</span>Consistency</a><a href="#/verdicts-move-with-things-that-should-not-matter"><span>1.2</span>Robustness</a><a href="#/agreement-with-people-does-not-transfer"><span>1.3</span>Transfer</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/a-fluent-explanation-is-not-proof"><span>1.4</span>Explanations</a></nav>
<div class="j2-split j2-split-even">
  <div class="j2-panel">
    <p class="j2-colhead">Did the judge point to the right step, for the right reason?</p>
    <p class="j2-metric">Right step and right reason, as checked by people</p>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">GPT-OSS-120B, τ-bench retail</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:58%"></span></span><b>58%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">GPT-OSS-120B, DA-Code</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:60%"></span></span><b>60%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Qwen3-235B, τ-bench retail</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:63%"></span></span><b>63%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Qwen3-235B, DA-Code</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-bad" style="width:43%"></span></span><b>43%</b></div>
    <p class="j2-src">Only about half the time. 1,131 human labels on judge explanations (<a href="../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/">Pisupati et al. 2026</a>). GPT-OSS at high reasoning effort.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="j2-side">
    <p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>More thinking gave fewer false alarms, but the bad reasons stayed the same.</b> False alarms fell from 187 to 68. Right step with a bad reason did not fall (109 and 112).</p>
    <p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>Nobody checked what the judges missed.</b> So the real picture may be worse.</p>
    <p class="j2-strong fragment" data-fragment-index="3">In Part 3, your evidence ID shows where the judge looked. It doesn't prove the judge was right. That part is still your job.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Explanations are part of a judge's output, and they fail separately from the score. A judge can flag the right step for the wrong reason, or the wrong step with a convincing reason. Part 2 called this rationalisation; here is how often it happens on agent tasks.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on the Spot On rates, then (1) more reasoning, (2) precision only, and (3) what this means for Part 3.
- Counsel: people labelled spans that open-weight judges had flagged on τ-bench retail (115 tasks) and DA-Code (50 tasks): Spot On (right place, right reason), Poor Reasoning (right place, bad reason) or Should Not Have Flagged. Table 2 has 1,131 labels: 555 Spot On, 289 Poor Reasoning, 287 Should Not Have Flagged. Spot On rates: Qwen3 43% on DA-Code and 63% on τ-bench retail; GPT-OSS-120B at high effort 60% and 58% ([Pisupati et al. 2026](../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/)).
- Reasoning effort: Should Not Have Flagged was 68 at high effort and 187 at low; Poor Reasoning was 112 and 109. Self-preference tests were not significant.
- Agreement among the three annotators was α ≈ 0.78 on 15 triple-labelled trajectories; the rest were labelled once. The DA-Code slice was chosen to be easier.
- Part 1 defined meta-evaluation with this paper: judging the judges. The Part 3 app requires valid evidence message IDs, and counts a malformed result as an evaluation error; it does not check that the evidence supports the claim (workshop/README.md).
:::

```{=html}
<p class="j2-sec-goal"><span>Learning goal 2</span>Even if the judge is a perfect tool, what can it not see?</p>
<p class="j2-colhead j2-sec-head">In this section</p>
<ol class="j2-sec-list">
  <li><a href="#/a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory"><span>2.1</span>A good final answer can hide a bad path</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse"><span>2.2</span>The rubric is part of the measurement</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result"><span>2.3</span>A score alone is not a result</a></li>
  <li><a href="#/what-the-part-3-exercise-could-not-show"><span>2.4</span>Our own exercise</a></li>
</ol>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Section 1 asked whether a judge is a good instrument. This section asks what even a good instrument cannot see: steps it is not shown, the choices built into the rubric, the cost and variance a single score hides, and the limits of the Part 3 exercise itself.
:::

## A good final answer can hide a bad path {#a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 2, Limitations: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/limitations-what-a-judge-score-cannot-tell-you"><span>2</span>Limitations</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory"><span>2.1</span>The path</a><a href="#/a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse"><span>2.2</span>The rubric</a><a href="#/a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result"><span>2.3</span>The score</a><a href="#/what-the-part-3-exercise-could-not-show"><span>2.4</span>Our exercise</a></nav>
<div class="j2-grid j2-g3">
  <div class="j2-cd"><span class="j2-cd-k">Shortcut</span><b>The result said: success</b><p>An agent found the benchmark's answers and just reported them. The final answer cannot show this (<a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-cd-k">Hidden error</span><b>The error is at step 14</b><p>The agent passes a wrong value to a tool. If the judge only reads the final answer, it never sees step 14 (<a href="../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/">Voss 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-cd-k">Many turns</span><b>No single turn fails. The conversation fails.</b><p>Over many turns, the agent slowly forgets things or mixes them up (<a href="../../bibliography/guan-2025-multiturn-survey/">Guan et al. 2025</a>).</p></div>
</div>
<div class="j2-note fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><b>Don't just check the final answer.</b> Give the judge the whole path, score each step, and read some cases that passed, not only the ones that failed (<a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>).</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Part 1 argued that agents must be judged on the trace, not only the reply. This slide is the limitation behind that: three kinds of failure that a score on the final answer cannot see.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on the shortcut, then (1) the hidden step, (2) many turns, and (3) what to do.
- Chen et al.: the same outcome can be reached by different trajectories, including shortcuts, so an outcome score does not say which behaviour was measured. Their Figure 11 is a fictional log marked as a success, in which the agent opened the benchmark's answers and reported them; they call it search-time contamination. They recommend checking an autograder against human-labelled holdouts and reviewing a sample of the cases the judge passed ([Chen et al. 2026](../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/)).
- Voss: a template judge maps columns such as input and output before anyone has seen the failure; if the failure is a stale argument at step 14, a judge pointed at the final answer never sees it ([Voss 2026](../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/)).
- Guan et al.: multi-turn agents add failure modes such as context drift, memory overwrites and compound tool-use errors that single-turn rubrics miss ([Guan et al. 2025](../../bibliography/guan-2025-multiturn-survey/)).
- Part 2's blind-spots row is the same lesson for criteria: one question over a whole trace caught about 54% of marked errors, seven separate judges 95% ([Jia et al. 2025](../../bibliography/jia-2025-agent-gpa/)).
:::

---

## The rubric is part of the measurement {#a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 2, Limitations: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/limitations-what-a-judge-score-cannot-tell-you"><span>2</span>Limitations</a><a href="#/a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory"><span>2.1</span>The path</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse"><span>2.2</span>The rubric</a><a href="#/a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result"><span>2.3</span>The score</a><a href="#/what-the-part-3-exercise-could-not-show"><span>2.4</span>Our exercise</a></nav>
<div class="j2-list">
  <div class="j2-li"><span class="j2-num">1</span><div><b>More rules do not make a better judge.</b> In one study, a rubric learned from data did worse than no rubric at all (<a href="../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/">Roy et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
  <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-num">2</span><div><b>If all the judges agree with each other, it doesn't mean they agree with people.</b> They can all be wrong together (<a href="../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/">Roy et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
  <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-num">3</span><div><b>When you fix one problem in a rubric, another problem can appear.</b> One fix raised accuracy. Another fix stopped tricks, but did not raise accuracy (<a href="../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/">Roy et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
  <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="j2-num">4</span><div><b>If your rule just says “quality”, the judge rewards long and beautiful answers,</b> not correct ones (<a href="../../bibliography/zhou-2024-mitigating-bias/">Zhou et al. 2024</a>).</div></div>
</div>
<div class="j2-note fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><b>Every time you change the rubric, treat it like changing the model.</b> Ask: what should this improve? Then test it again with people.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Part 2 taught how to write a rubric. The limitation is that a rubric is a measurement specification: each choice changes what is measured, and a reasonable-looking rubric can measure worse than none.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: one point per click: opens on more criteria, then (1) stable is not valid, (2) fixes pull apart, (3) vague criteria, and (4) treat an edit like a model change.
- PReMISE audits rubrics from several sources on four corpora. No source leads every column. Discovered PReMISE, before repair, is below the no-rubric baseline on every direct-verdict column; the preference repair moved accuracy from 65.0 to 68.6, a tenth under Auto-Rubric's 68.7, and on one judge (Qwen3-32B) it was still below no rubric, 65.8 against 66.4. The robustness repair cut the verified fool rate from 0.464 to 0.360, with α from 0.531 to 0.519 and no gain in accuracy. The authors say high α is a stability check, not evidence that the rubric matches people ([Roy et al. 2026](../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/)).
- A rubric tuned on a large judge is not guaranteed on a smaller one (same source).
- Zhou et al.: a judge asked for quality uses fluency, length and tone, because a pretrained score already likes them ([Zhou et al. 2024](../../bibliography/zhou-2024-mitigating-bias/)).
- Link to Part 3: participants edited rubrics between rounds. If the pass rate moved with the rubric while the traces stayed the same, the rubric was part of the measurement. Part 2 showed criteria drift in practice: 5 of 9 practitioners changed their criteria after grading outputs ([Shankar et al. 2024](../../bibliography/shankar-2024-validators/)).
:::

---

## A score alone is not a result {#a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 2, Limitations: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/limitations-what-a-judge-score-cannot-tell-you"><span>2</span>Limitations</a><a href="#/a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory"><span>2.1</span>The path</a><a href="#/a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse"><span>2.2</span>The rubric</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result"><span>2.3</span>The score</a><a href="#/what-the-part-3-exercise-could-not-show"><span>2.4</span>Our exercise</a></nav>
<div class="j2-grid j2-g3">
  <div class="j2-cd"><span class="j2-cd-k">Cost</span><b>Same accuracy, very different cost</b><p>On a coding test, agents with similar accuracy had costs up to about 100 times different. Just trying again did as well as complex agents (<a href="../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/">Kapoor et al. 2024</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-cd-k">Spread</span><b>One run is just one sample</b><p>Small changes early in a long task can grow into big differences at the end (<a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-cd-k">Holdout</span><b>A test set the system has never seen</b><p>Out of 17 agent benchmarks, 7 had no holdout at all (<a href="../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/">Kapoor et al. 2024</a>).</p></div>
</div>
<div class="j2-note fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><b>Report the score with its cost, its spread and a holdout:</b> new cases, new tasks or a new domain.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** The limits of the number itself, whoever produced it. These apply to the agent's score and to the judge's: both are measurements with a cost, a variance and a test set.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on cost, then (1) variance, (2) holdouts, and (3) what to report.
- Kapoor et al.: on HumanEval (164 problems, each agent run five times), supposedly state-of-the-art agents did not significantly beat simple baselines such as retrying or escalating to a stronger model, and cost for similar accuracy differed by almost two orders of magnitude. Their survey of 17 agent benchmarks found 7 with no holdout set and no sign of one planned; of the 10 with holdouts, 5 held out at the right level of generality ([Kapoor et al. 2024](../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/)).
- Their holdout rule: distribution-specific benchmarks hold out samples, task-specific ones out-of-distribution samples, domain-general ones whole tasks, and fully general ones whole domains.
- Chen et al.: accuracy leaves out cost, latency and reliability; runs vary more for agents; and attribution is hard, because the same scaffold need not interact with every model the same way ([Chen et al. 2026](../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/)).
- Part 2 counted judge calls (2.4) and compared quality, latency and cost by method (4.5). This slide is the reporting side: a result without these is not comparable.
:::

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 2, Limitations: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/limitations-what-a-judge-score-cannot-tell-you"><span>2</span>Limitations</a><a href="#/a-good-final-answer-can-hide-a-bad-trajectory"><span>2.1</span>The path</a><a href="#/a-rubric-is-a-measurement-and-it-can-make-things-worse"><span>2.2</span>The rubric</a><a href="#/a-score-without-cost-variance-and-a-holdout-is-not-a-result"><span>2.3</span>The score</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/what-the-part-3-exercise-could-not-show"><span>2.4</span>Our exercise</a></nav>
<table class="j2-tbl">
  <thead><tr><th>In Part 3</th><th>So we can't say</th><th>To fix it</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>1. The traces were synthetic, not real (10 traces)</td><td>how the judge does on real data</td><td>use a sample of real traces</td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><td>2. We had no human labels</td><td>whether the judge agrees with people</td><td>label a sample; report κ per criterion</td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><td>3. The judge scored everything in one request</td><td>whether it ignored later messages when scoring an earlier step</td><td>one request per step</td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><td>4. The pass mark of 4 was just a starting point</td><td>whether 4 is the right line</td><td>set it from labelled examples</td></tr>
    <tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><td>5. We used only one judge model</td><td>whether another model gives the same result</td><td>rerun with a second model family</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<p class="j2-strong fragment" data-fragment-index="5">Your Part 3 numbers show how the method works. They are not proof that the agent or the judge is good.</p>
<p class="j2-src">Exercise design from the workshop README. The scenarios and starter criteria are examples to edit, not an answer key.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** The same honesty applied to our own exercise. Part 3 was built to teach the method in an hour, so it leaves out what a real evaluation needs. Each row names what is missing and the step that would supply it.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: one row per click: opens on synthetic traces, then (1) no human labels, (2) one request, (3) the pass mark, (4) one judge model, and (5) what the numbers are.
- From workshop/README.md: three rounds of 4, 3 and 3 traces; agent tools are recorded fixtures, not live integrations; the variants are synthetic, with no preset scores or expected answers.
- One request per trace evaluates all targets, so the per-tool-call instruction “and evidence validation do not guarantee that the model ignores later context” (workshop/README.md). That is a design trade-off for cost: one call per trace in place of one per target.
- A trace passes only if every applicable criterion meets its threshold, initially 4. Means and pass rates use successful judge responses; errors are shown separately (workshop/README.md).
- The fixes are the checklist in section 3.1. The people who want to go further can take the app's report JSON and label a sample themselves.
:::

## Eight steps before you trust a judge {#before-you-trust-a-judge-a-checklist .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 3, Good practice, future: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/good-practice-and-future-directions"><span>3</span>Good practice, future</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/before-you-trust-a-judge-a-checklist"><span>3.1</span>Eight steps</a><a href="#/agent-as-a-judge-promising-and-not-yet-proven"><span>3.2</span>Agent-as-a-judge</a><a href="#/open-research-questions"><span>3.3</span>Open questions</a></nav>
<div class="j2-split j2-split-even">
  <div class="j2-list j2-list-sm">
    <p class="j2-colhead">Test the tool</p>
    <div class="j2-li"><span class="j2-num">1</span><div><b>Label a sample.</b> Compare with people using agreement corrected for chance (<a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/le-2026-sage/">Le et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-num">2</span><div><b>Run negative controls.</b> Give an empty answer, or just “Yes” (<a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-num">3</span><div><b>Test one bias at a time.</b> Change the order. Change the length (<a href="../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/">Ye et al. 2024</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="j2-num">4</span><div><b>Repeat, and report the spread</b> (<a href="../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/">Wang et al. 2024</a>).</div></div>
  </div>
  <div class="j2-list j2-list-sm">
    <p class="j2-colhead">Run it like real software</p>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><span class="j2-num">5</span><div><b>Give the judge a reference answer</b> when correctness matters (<a href="../../bibliography/krumdick-2025-no-free-labels/">Krumdick et al. 2025</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="5"><span class="j2-num">6</span><div><b>Read the evidence,</b> and check some passes, not only the failures (<a href="../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/">Pisupati et al. 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="6"><span class="j2-num">7</span><div><b>Version your judge.</b> When the model, the prompt or the rubric changes, run your test set again (<a href="../../bibliography/winston-2026-production-judges/">Winston 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/hong-2026-rulers/">Hong et al. 2026</a>).</div></div>
    <div class="j2-li fragment" data-fragment-index="7"><span class="j2-num">8</span><div><b>Report the cost</b> with every score (<a href="../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/">Kapoor et al. 2024</a>).</div></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Sections 1 and 2 turned into eight things a team can do before trusting a judge. The first four check the judge as an instrument; the last four are how teams that run judges in production keep them honest.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: one item per click: opens on item 1, then (1) to (7) items 2 to 8.
- 1: raw agreement flatters weak judges; judges with over 80–90% raw agreement still misjudged accuracy by 10–20 points, and Scott's π told them apart ([Thakur et al. 2024](../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/)). SAGE reports κ 0.77 against experts' 0.83 with each other ([Le et al. 2026](../../bibliography/le-2026-sage/)).
- 2: dummy answers are a zero-annotation sanity check anyone can run ([Thakur et al. 2024](../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/)).
- 3: change only one thing and see whether the verdict moves; randomise order, separate generator and judge, hide identities ([Ye et al. 2024](../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/)).
- 4: close cases flip ([Wang et al. 2024](../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/)); section 1.1.
- 5: expert references largely fixed the “agrees only when it knows” pattern ([Krumdick et al. 2025](../../bibliography/krumdick-2025-no-free-labels/)).
- 6: grade the explanation, not only the verdict ([Pisupati et al. 2026](../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/)); review a sample of the cases the judge passed ([Chen et al. 2026](../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/)).
- 7: Winston re-runs a canary set whenever the judge model changes ([Winston 2026](../../bibliography/winston-2026-production-judges/)); RULERS locks the rubric into one versioned bundle ([Hong et al. 2026](../../bibliography/hong-2026-rulers/)).
- 8: accuracy without cost can rank first a system nobody would deploy ([Kapoor et al. 2024](../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/)).
- Industry tooling: of 17 observability tools surveyed, only 4 were built for agents; 13 of the 15 compared support evaluation, and 6 runtime guardrails ([Dong et al. 2024](../../bibliography/dong-2024-agentops/)). Check that a platform records tool calls and plan steps, not only model calls.
:::

## Agent-as-a-judge: promising, but not yet proven {#agent-as-a-judge-promising-and-not-yet-proven .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 3, Good practice, future: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/good-practice-and-future-directions"><span>3</span>Good practice, future</a><a href="#/before-you-trust-a-judge-a-checklist"><span>3.1</span>Eight steps</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/agent-as-a-judge-promising-and-not-yet-proven"><span>3.2</span>Agent-as-a-judge</a><a href="#/open-research-questions"><span>3.3</span>Open questions</a></nav>
<div class="j2-split j2-split-even">
  <div class="j2-panel">
    <p class="j2-colhead">An agent judge can open files, run tests, and check each step</p>
    <p class="j2-metric">Agreement with experts, 55 coding tasks</p>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Majority of 3 experts</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-ref" style="width:94.3%"></span></span><b>94.3%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Agent judge</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf" style="width:90.2%"></span></span><b>90.2%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">A single expert</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-ref" style="width:85.7%"></span></span><b>85.7%</b></div>
    <div class="j2-bar"><span class="j2-bl">Normal LLM judge</span><span class="j2-bt"><span class="j2-bf j2-bf-bad" style="width:70.8%"></span></span><b>70.8%</b></div>
    <p class="j2-src"><a href="../../bibliography/zhuge-2025-agent-as-judge/">Zhuge et al. 2025</a>, as reported by <a href="../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/">Voss 2026</a></p>
  </div>
  <div class="j2-side">
    <p class="j2-colhead fragment" data-fragment-index="1">But, it's early</p>
    <ul class="j2-facts">
      <li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>Only one benchmark.</b> 55 coding tasks.</li>
      <li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>Memory spread mistakes.</b> One early mistake spread to later cases.</li>
      <li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><b>Results change from run to run,</b> and it may prefer longer runs.</li>
      <li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><b>It costs more.</b> Running a full agent for every evaluation costs more than one call.</li>
    </ul>
    <p class="j2-strong fragment" data-fragment-index="5">A new tool: test it against people, like any other judge.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** The main direction in agent evaluation: use an agent, which can open files, run checks and gather evidence, to judge another agent's steps, not only its final answer. The first results are strong and narrow.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: opens on the alignment figures, then (1) to (4) one open question per click, and (5) a new instrument.
- Zhuge et al. built DevAI, 55 automated AI development tasks with 365 hierarchical requirements, and found the agent judge “dramatically outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and is as reliable as” their human baseline ([Zhuge et al. 2025](../../bibliography/zhuge-2025-agent-as-judge/)).
- The figures on the slide are from the Arize post's chart of that benchmark: agent judge 90.2%, LLM judge 70.8%, average individual expert 85.7%, majority of three experts 94.3%. The experts disagreed with each other 10% to 30% of the time before debate. Cost on that benchmark: about US\$31 of API calls against nearly US\$1,300 of expert time ([Voss 2026](../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/)). Part 2 used the cost figure in 4.5.
- Voss lists the reliability questions rather than measuring them: production traffic has no expert consensus, a full agent per evaluation has a cost, the same judge differs across runs, and later work is finding a bias toward longer trajectories ([Voss 2026](../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/)).
- In Voss's layered model, the agent judge sits between the LLM judge and the person, for trajectory failures nobody wrote a check for (Part 2, 4.5).
:::

## Six open questions {#open-research-questions .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<nav class="j2-strip" aria-label="Section 3, Good practice, future: where this slide sits"><a class="j2-strip-sec" href="#/good-practice-and-future-directions"><span>3</span>Good practice, future</a><a href="#/before-you-trust-a-judge-a-checklist"><span>3.1</span>Eight steps</a><a href="#/agent-as-a-judge-promising-and-not-yet-proven"><span>3.2</span>Agent-as-a-judge</a><a class="is-on" aria-current="true" href="#/open-research-questions"><span>3.3</span>Open questions</a></nav>
<div class="j2-grid j2-g3">
  <div class="j2-cd"><span class="j2-cd-k">Agent traces</span><b>How good are judges at checking agent traces?</b><p>We have only a few test sets so far (<a href="../../bibliography/lu-2025-agentrewardbench/">Lù et al. 2025</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/peng-2026-ruverbench/">Peng et al. 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/">Pisupati et al. 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-cd-k">Conversations</span><b>How do we test memory and long conversations?</b><p>Very few benchmarks do this (<a href="../../bibliography/guan-2025-multiturn-survey/">Guan et al. 2025</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-cd-k">Real products</span><b>How do we judge real traffic without labels?</b><p>In real products, there is no answer key (<a href="../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/">Voss 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/mohammadi-2025-benchmark-survey/">Mohammadi et al. 2025</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="j2-cd-k">Rubrics</span><b>How do we design rubrics as real measurement tools?</b><p>Not just lists of nice words (<a href="../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/">Roy et al. 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/hong-2026-rulers/">Hong et al. 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><span class="j2-cd-k">Benchmarks</span><b>How do we build benchmarks whose scores really mean what they say?</b><p>Right holdouts, no leaked answers, and knowing what caused a change (<a href="../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/">Kapoor et al. 2024</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>).</p></div>
  <div class="j2-cd fragment" data-fragment-index="5"><span class="j2-cd-k">Cost</span><b>How do we make cheap judges that stay accurate over time?</b><p>Juries of small models, smaller trained judges, and sending hard cases to people (<a href="../../bibliography/verga-2024-juries/">Verga et al. 2024</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/le-2026-sage/">Le et al. 2026</a>; <a href="../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/">Wang et al. 2024</a>).</p></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**About this slide:** Six open problems for trustworthy agent evaluation, each with the work to start from. They come from the limitations in sections 1 and 2.

**Presenter notes:**

- Builds: one question per click: opens on trajectories, then (1) conversations, (2) production, (3) validity, (4) benchmarks, and (5) cost.
- Trajectories: AgentRewardBench found no judge above 70% precision on web-agent success ([Lù et al. 2025](../../bibliography/lu-2025-agentrewardbench/)); RuVerBench found judges crediting partly met rubric items on coding traces ([Peng et al. 2026](../../bibliography/peng-2026-ruverbench/)); Counsel checks the judges' critiques ([Pisupati et al. 2026](../../bibliography/pisupati-2026-counsel/)).
- Conversations: benchmarks that jointly test long-horizon memory, dynamic re-planning when a tool fails mid-conversation, and multi-turn safety are still sparse ([Guan et al. 2025](../../bibliography/guan-2025-multiturn-survey/)). Part 1's multi-turn attack example is the safety case.
- Production: spot-checks against people remain because live traffic has no consensus ([Voss 2026](../../bibliography/voss-2026-agent-as-judge/)); offline datasets are the cheaper and less faithful option ([Mohammadi et al. 2025](../../bibliography/mohammadi-2025-benchmark-survey/)).
- Validity: section 2.2 ([Roy et al. 2026](../../bibliography/roy-2026-premise/)); evidence-grounded scoring with a locked rubric is one response ([Hong et al. 2026](../../bibliography/hong-2026-rulers/)).
- Benchmarks: section 2.3 ([Kapoor et al. 2024](../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/); [Chen et al. 2026](../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/)).
- Cost: a jury of three small models at 7–8× lower cost than GPT-4 Turbo ([Verga et al. 2024](../../bibliography/verga-2024-juries/)); SAGE's distilled student for production volume ([Le et al. 2026](../../bibliography/le-2026-sage/)); routing the least stable 20% to people ([Wang et al. 2024](../../bibliography/wang-2024-not-fair/)). All from Part 2; the open question is how to keep them calibrated as the agent and its traffic change.
- The reading list has more recent agent-judge benchmarks (AgentJudgeBench, MobileJudgeBench, trajectory-judge). Their citations are not yet verified in the bibliography, so they are not on the slide.
:::

## Four things to take home {#recap-what-to-take-home .j2-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="j2-recap">
  <div class="j2-rc"><span class="j2-num">1</span><b>Reliability</b><p>Your judge can change its mind, can be fooled by small things, and agrees with people only on the task it was tested on.</p><span class="j2-use">Try: repeat it, swap the answers, and try a silly answer like “Yes”</span></div>
  <div class="j2-rc fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="j2-num">2</span><b>Limitations</b><p>A good final answer can hide a bad path. The rubric is part of the measurement. A score needs cost, spread and a holdout.</p><span class="j2-use">Try: label some of your own traces</span></div>
  <div class="j2-rc fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="j2-num">3</span><b>Good practice</b><p>Compare with people, version your judge, read the evidence, check some passes, and report the cost.</p><span class="j2-use">Try: the eight-step checklist</span></div>
  <div class="j2-rc fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="j2-num">4</span><b>The future</b><p>Agent judges, checking agent traces, long conversations, real traffic, and better rubrics.</p><span class="j2-use">Pick: one open question that fits your work</span></div>
</div>
<div class="j2-running fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><b>The judge is a measuring tool.</b> Check it before you trust the number, and keep checking every time something changes.</div>
<p class="j2-src">To read further, start with <a href="../../bibliography/thakur-2024-judging-the-judges/">Thakur et al. 2024</a>, <a href="../../bibliography/ye-2024-justice-or-prejudice/">Ye et al. 2024</a>, <a href="../../bibliography/kapoor-2024-agents-that-matter/">Kapoor et al. 2024</a> and <a href="../../bibliography/chen-2026-emerging-trends/">Chen et al. 2026</a>, or the full <a href="../../bibliography/">bibliography</a>. The <a href="../../hands-on/">hands-on app</a> stays online after today.</p>
```
